scan.summary: This is an internal operating record: one month of daily pre-shift inspection entries for a single propane forklift (unit FL-2) at the Portland warehouse, covering Sep 1 through Sep 18, 2026, with operator initials and an hour-meter reading on each line. A log like this is judged on whether it is complete and current, not against a written standard — it is the evidence you would hand an Oregon OSHA inspector to show the truck was examined before use and that defects were acted on. As it stands it has calendar gaps, a recorded defect with no closing entry, no supervisor sign-off, and no entries for the past week and a half.
scan.freshness_note: The last entry is 2026-09-18, nine days before today (2026-09-27). Five working days (Sep 21–25) have passed with no recorded inspection. Ask for the current sheet — either the rest of September or an October sheet — before treating this as the live record.

gaps.title: No inspection entries for Sep 3 and Sep 4 although the truck ran
gaps.description: The log jumps from Sep 2 to Sep 7 with no rows for Thursday Sep 3 or Friday Sep 4, both ordinary working days. The hour meter rose 15 hours across that break (4,819 to 4,834), so the truck was used on days with no recorded examination.
gaps.fix: Have the supervisor and the two operators reconstruct what happened on Sep 3–4 and add a dated late entry, or a dated note on the sheet saying the inspection was missed and why. Do not backfill ticks as if the checks happened. Then put a daily control in place — no keys issued until the line is signed.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — trucks examined before being placed in service, at least daily; adopted in Oregon under OAR 437-002-0220 (Adoption by Reference) with additional state rules at OAR 437-002-0227. I am confident in the federal cite; the OAR numbering is my best reading.
gaps.quote: The hour meter rises between Sep 2 (4,819) and Sep 7 (4,834), which shows the truck ran on the missing days.

gaps.title: Horn defect recorded Sep 9 with no repair or return-to-service entry
gaps.description: The Sep 9 row carries an X under Horn with the note 'Horn not working'. Nothing on either page records that the truck was taken out of service, that the horn was repaired, or who released it back to use. The next row, Sep 10, shows the horn ticked as OK, which implies a repair that is nowhere documented.
gaps.fix: Attach the work order, invoice or mechanic's note for the horn repair to this sheet, with the date and who returned the truck to service. If no repair record exists, have the person who fixed it write a dated statement now. Add a 'defect closed — date / by whom' column so the loop is closed on the sheet itself.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) (defects when found shall be immediately reported and corrected) and 29 CFR 1910.178(p)(1) (truck in unsafe condition removed from service until restored to safe operating condition)

gaps.title: Supervisor review line left blank
gaps.description: The sheet provides a supervisor review and date line at the foot of page 2 and it is unsigned and undated. Nobody above the operators has signed off on a month that contains a missed-day gap and an open defect.
gaps.fix: Have the warehouse supervisor review the sheet, resolve the Sep 3–4 and Sep 9 items, then sign and date it. Make the sign-off weekly rather than monthly so gaps are caught within days.

gaps.title: No entries after Sep 18 — the record is nine days stale
gaps.description: The last line is Sep 18. Sep 21, 22, 23, 24 and 25 were working days with no recorded inspection. Either the sheet has not been collected, the truck has been idle, or the checks are not being done.
gaps.fix: Produce the current sheet today. If the truck genuinely sat unused, write a dated line on the sheet saying so — an out-of-service or idle note is a legitimate answer, an empty grid is not.

gaps.title: Only day-shift checks recorded at a site your records describe as multi-shift
gaps.description: Every one of the nineteen rows is marked 'Day'. Your company record set says the Portland site runs more than one shift. If FL-2 is used on a later shift, that shift's examination is not being recorded — and where a truck runs round the clock the examination is required after each shift, not once a day.
gaps.fix: Confirm whether FL-2 is used outside day shift. If it is, add a row per shift with the shift operator's initials. If it genuinely runs day shift only, write that on the sheet so the single-shift pattern is explained rather than assumed.
gaps.citation: 29 CFR 1910.178(q)(7) — where industrial trucks are used on a round-the-clock basis they shall be examined after each shift
gaps.quote: Date Shift Hours Tires Forks Mast Horn Lights Belt Brakes Steering LPG Ext. Plate Guard Operator Notes

Medium confidence on the Oregon adoption citation — Oregon OSHA plainly enforces 1910.178 with additional state rules at OAR 437-002-0227 (Oregon OSHA's own forklift fact sheet pairs the two), but I have not confirmed that OAR 437-002-0220 is the exact adoption-by-reference section for Subdivision N; treat that number as my best reading. One correction to the earlier reading: counting from the Sep 18 entry to today, five working days are missing (Sep 21–25), not seven — the finding is the same, the count is not. Also note Sep 7, 2026 was Labor Day and was worked, while Sep 3 and 4 were ordinary working days with no entry. The multi-shift finding is inferred: the sheet itself only ever says 'Day', and the multi-shift characterisation comes from your other records, not from this document. I have not judged whether the checklist items themselves are adequate — OSHA does not prescribe a format.
